claims.text: The proposed framework combines ab initio calculations using special quasi-random structures with kinetic Monte Carlo simulations.
Ab initio calculations with SQS have been applied to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
SQS models can represent a statistically random solid solution of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr.
The bulk alloy contains a statistically random population of native point defects.
The framework will explicitly model the electronic structure effects of point defects and 1 wt.% oxygen.
Kinetic Monte Carlo simulations can capture the temperature-dependent evolution of defect scattering in this alloy.
Adding 1 wt.% oxygen produces local lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Impurity and static-defect scattering dominate electronic conduction between approximately 0 and 200 K.
Static defect and impurity scattering reduce carrier mobility at low temperatures.
Phonon scattering and thermally activated defect evolution become significant between 300 and 1200 K.
Phonon scattering combined with dynamically evolving defect distributions alters high-temperature electron transport.
Explicitly simulating defect, impurity, and phonon scattering will predict conductivity more accurately than perfect-crystal models.
The predicted conductivity will differ markedly from predictions made by perfect-crystal analytical models.
At a held-out 400 K benchmark, the framework will predict experimental conductivity within 10%.
Existing perfect, defect-free crystal models often differ from experimental conductivity by more than 20%.
The framework is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing up to 1 wt.% oxygen over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Predictive accuracy may deteriorate outside the specified temperature ranges or at substantially higher impurity concentrations.
Defect population statistics and scattering-rate parameters may materially affect convergence and predictive precision.
A conductivity error greater than 20% at 400 K is specified as the result that would falsify the hypothesis.
